elements.element: Customer pays no liquidated damages or penalties.
elements.evidence: Revised § 13.5 retains "Customer acknowledges that the Termination for Convenience Fee is a reasonable approximation of such damages and shall be deemed to be liquidated damages and not a penalty," and § 11.1 still requires Customer to pay an early termination fee, so a Customer-payable liquidated amount survives. The preferred level is expressly not the claimed target.

elements.element: Any Customer-payable liquidated amount is only an early-termination fee.
elements.evidence: The separate "Termination for Cause Fee" is gone: revised § 11.2(A) now says Customer "shall pay M&I the Termination for Convenience Fee determined and payable as set forth in Section 11.1 above, and no other termination fee, liquidated damages or penalty," and § 13.5 now references only the Termination for Convenience Fee, which § 11.1 defines as "an early termination fee." Retained § 11.1 unamortized Conversion costs and reasonable Expenses are actual-cost reimbursements, not liquidated amounts.

elements.element: The early-termination fee is capped at three months of fees.
elements.evidence: § 11.1 as revised sets the fee "in an amount equal to three (3) times the average monthly Fees payable by Customer during the three (3) months prior to the Effective Date of Termination," replacing the percentage of "Estimated Remaining Value" (months remaining × monthly base/average fees). That is three months of fees and does not exceed the fallback threshold.

elements.element: The early-termination fee is the sole liquidated amount payable by Customer.
elements.evidence: New final sentence of § 13.5: "The Termination for Convenience Fee is the sole liquidated amount payable by Customer under this Agreement." This is unconditional and, with the deletion of the Cause Fee formula, leaves no other retained liquidated formula in the cited text.

elements.element: The early-termination fee is the sole liquidated amount payable by Customer.
elements.evidence: Not a preferred-level element; assessed at fallback level above. Listed here only for completeness — the preferred checklist contains a single element (no liquidated damages or penalties at all), which the retained § 13.5 liquidated-damages characterisation defeats.

reasons: Fallback level is substantively complete: a single early-termination fee, quantified at three months' average Fees, expressly declared the sole liquidated amount payable by Customer. Preferred level is not reached because § 13.5 still deems the fee liquidated damages payable by Customer.

Minimality defect — duplicated operative term: the sole-liquidated-amount element is delivered by the new final sentence of § 13.5. The added tail in § 11.2(A) ("and no other termination fee, liquidated damages or penalty") restates the same operative exclusivity a second time. Delete the § 11.2(A) tail and rely on § 13.5, or vice versa, but do not enact the exclusivity twice.

Intent defect — contradictory retained sentence: § 11.1 still provides that "The Termination for Convenience Fee shall apply to any early termination of this Agreement other than pursuant to an Event of Default on the part of Customer or M&I," while revised § 11.2(A) now makes that very fee payable when M&I terminates following Customer's Event of Default. Repair by amending the § 11.1 scoping sentence (e.g., renaming the charge a single "Early Termination Fee" applicable to any early termination, including one following an Event of Default by Customer, other than under Section 11.3) so the two sections do not conflict on whether the fee is owed on a default termination.

Housekeeping to confirm (not a level failure): "Estimated Remaining Value" (Definition N) is left intact and is now unused in the cited provisions — verify no other section relies on it, and note that the new cap's temporal anchor is the Effective Date of Termination rather than the definition's "event giving rise to termination rights," which is acceptable for the three-months-of-fees element but should be stated deliberately.

Severity remains high: the pre-redline construct (two fees, each a percentage of remaining contract value and each carved out of the § 13.4 limitation, one triggered by Customer default) sat at or near walk-away, so the redline is warranted even though the two drafting defects above must be cured.
